newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: S.E.Asian Cocoa - Prices higher on New York gains.
newsitem.headline: S.E.Asian Cocoa - Prices higher on New York gains.

text.p: Southeast Asian cocoa prices were higher on Wednesday, helped by overnight gains in New York and tight supply in Indonesia, traders said. Steady demand for cocoa beans in Malaysia also supported prices.
"Demand in Malaysia is still intact," said a trader in the main growing area of Tawau in Sabah, eastern Malaysia.
"Domestic production is not enough to meet demand from the 11 active grinders in the country. A lot of beans are being imported mainly from Indonesia," he said.
Traders said prices were fundamentally supported by a bad early crop for 1997, which is expected to slash Malaysia's usual mid-year cocoa harvest by 60 percent.

On Wednesday, the Malaysian Cocoa Board quoted Standard Malaysian Cocoa (SMC) Grade 1A out of Tawau at an average of 3,405 ringgit a tonne and Grade 1B, also out of Tawau, at an average of 3,355 ringgit.
Compared to Tuesday, the 1A was up 65 ringgit and 1B up 100 ringgit. But if compared to a week ago, both the grades were down 20 ringgit.
On Wednesday, trading houses quoted the 1A at around 3,440 ringgit and the 1B at 3,390.
Traders said gains, however, could be limited due to fears of a fresh speculative sell-off in New York.
"The New York market is a bit nervous at the moment and the uncertainty is spilling over to the local market," said a trader at a cocoa mill.
In Indonesia, supply was tight despite the ongoing main crop harvest, traders said.

The traders said fair average quality (FAQ) cocoa beans were quoted at 3,000-3,100 rupiah/kg in Ujung Pandang, capital of the key growing region of South Sulawesi, compared with 2,950-2,980 rupiah on Tuesday and 2,975-3,000 a week ago.
"The increase in New York helped to firm up prices here," one trader said. "The market is a little slow, but there are players who are buying to meet contracts."
The traders said supply was getting tight, but added that the situation could change as the main crop harvest gathers speed next month.
"Feedback from the districts show that supply is tight," one trader said. "Things might pick up as the harvest proceeds."
